prize_parts.citation: for credibly identified evidence on how import competition, alongside technological change, reshapes local labour markets, employment and earnings

statement.case_for: I keep B044 as my preferred single part, with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. Two things changed since round 1. First, I narrowed the citation so that it rests on the trade-shock and local-labour-market evidence, where the three-author attribution is clean. Technological change appears as context and is not claimed as a separate achievement. This answers the chair's question and the point made by Krusell, Hjalmarsson and Strömberg that the task lineage runs through people outside the credited set (Acemoglu, Levy, Murnane, Katz). Second, I have replaced B017 with B002 as my second alternative. I demoted B017 in round 1 because of its proximity to the 2024 institutions prize, and listing it again would be inconsistent. On the merits, the China-shock papers show with a transparent design that import competition causes persistent employment, earnings and adjustment losses in exposed local labour markets. The design has been replicated across countries. It changed how economists and policymakers think about who bears the costs of trade integration. The core papers are about thirteen years old, and the refinements so far have qualified magnitudes without overturning the central finding. The criterion I rank first is credibility of identification together with demonstrated change in what the field and policy treat as known. I regard B044 and B040 as close. B040 wins on conceptual generality and age. B044 wins on direct evidence, so it is not simply the case with less empirical risk. I do not find a coherent two-part configuration. Adding one B044 name to the B040 pair would split the credit for a jointly authored design and mis-describe it, and two full parts would exceed the three-person limit.
statement.case_against: B040 has the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, a single originating paper by two authors, and almost three decades of use. B044 rests on a research design and a body of empirical findings, not on one new conceptual framework. The shift-share identification has known inference problems. The size and persistence of the effects, and how much is trade rather than automation, are still contested. The trade-shock papers are younger than several rival candidates. The task-based strand and the trade-shock strand can reasonably be judged as two separate contributions, and my narrowed citation concedes part of this by not crediting the task framework as such. If the Committee puts conceptual breakthrough and age first, B040 is the stronger choice. My own training in causal inference and measurement may lead me to weight credible identification above conceptual generality, and I should state that.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B040 first with Kiyotaki and Moore and keeps B044 as his first alternative with only Autor and Hanson. He treats the task-based and China-shock strands as separable. He argues that B040 is less exposed on maturity than B044 because of the ongoing shift-share and persistence debates. He also says that excluding Gertler and Gilchrist should rest on the independent origin of the mechanism and not on earlier recognition.
responses.response: I agree that the strands are separable, and my narrower citation follows from that. I accept that B040 is less exposed on maturity measured in years. I do not think the shift-share debate is equivalent to an unsettled finding. The inference literature has mainly refined standard errors and magnitudes, while the qualitative result of persistent local losses has held. I still do not accept the Autor-Hanson pair. Dorn co-authored the central trade-shock papers, so dropping him would mis-describe a three-author design. If the Committee accepts that, the cap is not a constraint here. I also agree with your correction on Gertler and Gilchrist, because the exclusion should rest on the independent origin of the collateral-constraint mechanism. That improves my view of B040's attribution, and I still weigh it as less decisive than direct identification.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B040 first. He says the Kiyotaki-Moore pair is the clearest attribution, that overlap with the 2022 prize is the main risk, and that direct empirical validation is mixed. In round 1 he ranked B044 eighth because of recency and the identification debate, but said he now thinks that was somewhat low.
responses.response: I accept your attribution argument and I take your updated view of B044 as a real concession. I disagree that the validation gap is a minor weakness for B040. If the mechanism's quantitative size is contested, the prize would honour a theoretical idea whose empirical importance remains open. For B044 the equivalent uncertainty concerns magnitudes. The existence and persistence of local costs are credibly shown. On the 2022 overlap, I treat the difference in mechanism as real and not disqualifying. That is why B040 remains my first alternative. The gap between us is mostly about weighting, with clean attribution and age on your side and direct evidence on mine. I do not think either of us has an argument that should move the other.

responses.point: Krusell moved from B002 to B044 and anchors the citation on trade-shock evidence only. He argues that the task framework runs through Acemoglu, who is already a laureate, and that a separate part would be needed for the skill-bias strand, which is impractical under the cap. He also says that Katz should not replace Dorn.
responses.response: I follow you on the citation, and my narrowing reflects your argument. I would not move further and delete technological change entirely. The question of how technology and trade jointly shift labour demand is why the evidence matters to the field, and the citation can mention technology without crediting the task framework. I agree with you on Dorn and Katz. Katz's skill-bias contribution is an earlier strand that deserves its own recognition and does not fit in this citation. I also take your point that B002 is the least mature of the serious candidates, and I list it as an alternative only. Your move toward B044 is a scientific judgement and I do not treat it as support for mine.

responses.point: Dreber-Almenberg ranks B040 first and her main concern, as a metascience researcher, is that its quantitative and causal tests have been mixed. She would draft the citation around the mechanism and its influence on how credit cycles are modelled, not around empirical confirmation. She sees B044 as a close alternative if the two-strand question is settled.
responses.response: I agree with your drafting. A B040 citation worded around the mechanism and its influence on modelling is accurate and honest. Your metascience worry applies to both candidates in different ways. The collateral-constraint mechanism has weak direct tests. The China-shock result has been tested hard and has survived, which is the kind of replication record a metascience reading should reward. On the two-strand question you leave open, my answer is a narrower citation that credits the trade-shock evidence, with technology as context. I accept that this is a judgement. If you and others find it unpersuasive, I would not press the case that the task framework belongs in the prize.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B044 first and has now dropped Katz for Dorn. She says the best argument for centring the citation on trade-shock and labour-demand evidence is the Acemoglu lineage in the task framework. She is less persuaded that B017 should lead because of overlap with the 2024 prize.
responses.response: I agree with you on Katz and on the 2024 overlap, and I have acted on both, since B017 no longer features in my configuration. My residual difference with you is that I do not credit more of the task framework than my narrowed citation implies. If your wording keeps 'technological change and import competition' on equal footing, it implies Autor, Dorn and Hanson jointly established the task framework, and I do not think the record supports that. I would prefer a citation in which technological change is context and the credited contribution is the local-labour-market evidence, and I would ask you to consider that wording.

uncertainties: Whether the narrowed citation is acceptable or whether the Committee reads technological change as a separate achievement that should either be credited properly or left out.
How robust the persistence and size of China-shock effects are to alternative inference for shift-share designs, and how much of the adjustment is trade and how much automation.
Whether B044's empirical design carries enough conceptual weight, relative to a mechanism such as B040, for a prize of this kind.

How much the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises narrows the marginal case for B040, and whether its indirect empirical validation should count more heavily against it than the magnitude debate counts against B044.
Whether the trade-shock papers, at about thirteen years, are mature enough compared with B040's nearly thirty years.
My assessment draws on general knowledge and the supplied round-1 materials, not independent verification of citations, replication results or attribution.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for B044, B040 or B002 from the supplied profile. My listed collaborators and institutional ties (V-Dem core team, Rothstein, Holmberg, Hadenius, Dahlström, Lapuente, Bäck, Lindvall) are not credited names on the shortlist. My Stockholm University colleagues on the Committee (Hassler, Krusell, Boppart) are in a different department. I disclose that I am a political scientist, so B017 is close to my own field. It is now outside my configuration, and I do not treat that as a recusal basis. Research on the political consequences of trade exposure sits close to political science, which may make me more receptive to B044, and my methodological orientation toward causal identification may lead me to weight direct evidence more than conceptual generality. These are disclosed, not adjudicated.
